title: "Anomaly Detection"
description: "The identification of observations that differ substantially from expected patterns."
term: "Anomaly Detection"
letter: "A"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Anomaly detection finds observations that are unusual compared with a
baseline or the rest of the data. An anomaly may indicate a fault, fraud,
intrusion, data-quality problem, or simply a rare but valid event.

## Technical explanation

Methods include statistical thresholds, distance- or density-based
approaches, isolation methods, and models trained on normal examples.
Anomaly scores rank observations by how unusual they appear; a threshold
then converts scores into alerts. Labels are often sparse, and the meaning
of an anomaly depends on context.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

AI pipelines and deployed systems can use anomaly detection to surface
unexpected inputs, operational issues, or shifts in data. False alarms and
missed detections have different costs, so thresholds and response
procedures need to reflect the use case.

## How it works

The system learns or defines expected patterns, scores new observations,
and compares scores with a threshold or review policy. Teams validate the
method on representative data, account for seasonality and changing
baselines, and investigate alerts before treating them as incidents.

## Practical example

A service can monitor request latency and flag values far above its normal
range. The alert is a signal for investigation, not proof that a system
failure occurred.

## Common misconceptions

- An unusual point is not necessarily an error or malicious event.
- A low-frequency event can be important even if it is valid.
- Anomaly detection is not the same as classification when labeled classes
  are available and appropriate.
